A blunt mower blade tears the grass rather than cutting it, leaving a frayed, whitish tip on every leaf that browns off and lets in disease. Sharpen or swap the blade at least once a season, and the lawn shows the difference within a week of mowing.

Let a corner of the lawn grow long. An unmown patch left through spring and summer lets grasses flower and wildflowers seed, and the long sward shelters beetles, moths, and small mammals that the close-cropped rest of the garden offers nothing to.

Plant a mix of flowers that bloom in unbroken succession from the first warm days of spring to the last of autumn. A garden with nectar always on offer feeds bees and butterflies right through their active season, where a single summer flush leaves them hungry on either side.

Single, open flowers feed pollinators far better than tightly packed double blooms. The bee can reach the nectar and pollen of an open-faced flower easily, while a many-petalled double often offers little or nothing and is sometimes sterile altogether.

Leave the seedheads of plants like teasel, sunflower, and echinacea standing through autumn and winter. Goldfinches and other birds work them over for weeks, and the dry stems and hollow stalks shelter overwintering insects that would find a tidied border bare.

A log pile in a quiet, shady corner is one of the richest habitats a garden can offer. As the wood decays it feeds beetles, fungi, and woodlice, which in turn feed the birds, hedgehogs, and amphibians that hunt among the rotting timber.

Native plants and the local wildlife evolved together, so a hedge or border of native species feeds and shelters far more creatures than an exotic equivalent. The caterpillars that strip a native shrub a little are themselves the food that raises a brood of garden birds.

Cut a hedgehog highway, a small gap at the base of a fence, so the animals can roam between gardens on their nightly travels. A hedgehog needs to cover a wide area to find enough food, and a garden sealed off behind solid fencing is a dead end for it.

A shallow dish of water with a few stones for insects to land on, kept topped up and clean, helps wildlife through a dry spell. Bees, birds, and beetles all need to drink, and in a heatwave a reliable water source can matter as much as the flowers.

Avoid pesticides in a wildlife garden, even the organic ones, because a spray that kills the aphids also kills the ladybird larvae and lacewings that would have controlled them for free. Tolerate some damage and let the predators build up, and the garden balances itself.

Plant a tree, even a small one, if you possibly can. A single tree feeds and shelters more species than any other plant in the garden, offering blossom for pollinators, leaves for caterpillars, fruit and seeds for birds, and nesting sites in its branches.

Save seed only from open-pollinated or heirloom varieties, never from F1 hybrids. The seed of an F1 plant does not breed true; sow it and you get an unpredictable scramble of the parent types rather than a copy of the plant you saved it from.

Let the seed mature fully on the plant before you collect it. A pod, head, or fruit harvested too green carries seed that has not finished developing and will germinate poorly or not at all, so wait until the seed is plump, hard, and ripe.

Dry collected seed thoroughly before storing it. Spread it in a single layer somewhere warm, airy, and out of direct sun for a week or two, because any trapped moisture invites mould and shortens the seed's life dramatically in storage.

Saving tomato seed means a short fermentation. Scoop the seeds and their jelly into a jar of water and leave it a few days until a scummy mould forms; this dissolves the gel coat and the germination-inhibiting layer, after which the clean seed sinks and can be dried.

Store dried seed cool, dark, and dry, in paper envelopes inside an airtight tin or jar. A constant low temperature and the absence of moisture and light keep the seed viable for years, while a warm, damp shelf will see its vigour fade within a season.

Label every batch of saved seed at once with the variety and the year. An unlabelled packet is a mystery by spring, and noting the year matters because seed viability declines with age and you will want to sow the oldest packets first.

Beans and peas are the easiest crops for a beginner to save. They are self-pollinating, so cross-contamination between varieties is rare, and you simply leave a few pods on the plant to dry brown and papery, then shell out the seed.

To keep a variety pure, isolate it from others of the same species that might cross-pollinate it. Insect-pollinated crops like squash and brassicas cross readily, so grow only one variety, separate them by a good distance, or hand-pollinate and bag the flowers.

Test old seed before committing a whole bed to it. Roll ten seeds in a damp paper towel, keep it warm, and count how many sprout after a week or so; if only three come up, you know to sow that packet three times as thickly or not at all.

Saving your own seed year after year slowly adapts a variety to your particular garden. By always collecting from the strongest, healthiest, best-performing plants, you breed a strain that suits your soil and climate better with each passing season.

Read the kind of shade you have before choosing plants. Dry shade under a greedy tree is the hardest of all, damp shade in a cool corner the easiest, and dappled shade beneath a high canopy will grow far more than a gardener expects.

Hostas, ferns, and the woodland perennials are the backbone of a shade border. They evolved on the forest floor in exactly these conditions, and a planting of their bold and feathery leaves brings a lush, layered richness that flowers alone never could.

In a shady garden, foliage does the heavy lifting. Contrast the broad paddle of a hosta, the lace of a fern, the strap of an iris, and the heart-shaped leaf of an epimedium, and the border holds interest for months without depending on a brief flush of flower.

Pale flowers and variegated or silver leaves light up a dark corner. White, cream, and pale yellow seem to glow in low light, drawing the eye into a gloomy spot that a rich crimson or deep blue would simply vanish into.

Dry shade beneath a mature tree is starved of both light and water, since the tree's roots take the lion's share of the moisture. Improve it with plenty of organic matter, water new plants well until established, and choose tough survivors like epimedium, geranium, and ivy.

Make the most of spring in a deciduous wood or under leafy trees, when the canopy is still bare and light floods the ground. A carpet of woodland bulbs and early perennials does its whole year's growing and flowering before the leaves close overhead and the shade returns.

Many woodland plants prefer a humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil that mimics a forest floor deep in leaf litter. Mulch a shade border each year with leaf mould or compost, and the plants reward the cool, spongy root run with steady, healthy growth.

A pale-painted fence, a mirror, or light-coloured paving can bounce a surprising amount of light into a shady corner, lifting both the gardener's mood and the plants' performance. Even thinning a few branches overhead to let in dapple transforms what will grow.

Shade is a relief, not just a limitation. On a baking summer day a shaded seat is the most-used spot in the garden, the plants there never scorch or wilt, and a cool, green, ferny corner has a restful atmosphere a sun-drenched border cannot match.

Lift the canopy of an overgrown shrub or small tree by removing its lowest branches. Crown-lifting in this way lets light slant in underneath without losing the tree, and suddenly a band of ground that grew nothing is bright enough for a whole shade border.

Take softwood cuttings in late spring and early summer from the soft, flexible new growth. These root the fastest of all but wilt easily, so work quickly, keep them out of the sun, and put them in a propagator or under a cover to hold up the humidity until roots form.

A semi-ripe cutting, taken in late summer from growth that is firming up but not yet fully woody, is the most forgiving for a beginner. It is less prone to wilting than a softwood cutting and roots more readily than a hardwood one, a reliable middle path.

Make the cut cleanly just below a leaf node, the slight swelling where a leaf joins the stem, because that is where the cutting's rooting hormones concentrate and where new roots emerge most willingly. A cut between nodes roots far more reluctantly.

Strip the lower leaves from a cutting and shorten any large remaining ones by half. The bare lower stem goes into the compost, and reducing the leaf area cuts water loss through the foliage while the cutting has no roots to replace it.

Dip the base of a cutting in rooting hormone powder or gel to speed and improve the strike, especially for woodier subjects. Tap off the excess, since a thick clump of powder can do more harm than good, and a thin coating is all the cutting needs.

Use a free-draining, low-nutrient cutting compost, a mix of something like perlite and a little peat-free compost. Rich soil is the wrong medium; the cutting has no roots to take up feed, and the open, airy mix gives the new roots oxygen and stops the base rotting.

Keep cuttings in a humid atmosphere until they root, because with no roots they cannot replace the water they lose through their leaves. A clear bag over the pot, or a propagator lid, holds the moisture in, but air it occasionally to keep mould from taking hold.

Resist the urge to tug a cutting to see if it has rooted. A gentle test is fine once new growth appears at the tip, the surest sign that roots have formed below, and only then should the cutting be carefully potted on into its own container of proper compost.

Hardwood cuttings of shrubs and fruit are taken in late autumn from the year's mature, leafless wood and are the least demanding of all. Simply pushed into a slit trench of gritty soil outdoors, they need no propagator and root slowly over the following months.

Take more cuttings than you think you need, because not every one will strike, and a generous batch costs nothing but a little effort. From a single parent plant a tray of cuttings can fill a new hedge or stock a border for the price of an afternoon's work.

A cold frame is a halfway house between the greenhouse and the open garden. Through spring it hardens off seedlings, gradually acclimatizing them to outdoor conditions before they are planted out, and the slow transition spares them the check of a sudden move.

Prop the lid of a cold frame open on warm, sunny days so the heat does not build to a level that scorches and stresses the plants inside. Close it again in late afternoon to trap the day's warmth before the temperature falls overnight.

Site a cold frame against a south-facing wall to catch the low winter sun and the warmth the bricks store and release. A frame in that sheltered spot stays several degrees warmer than the open garden and extends the growing season at both ends of the year.

Through winter a cold frame protects hardy salads, overwintering vegetables, and dormant cuttings from the worst of the wet and cold. Throw an old blanket or a sheet of bubble wrap over the glass on the hardest nights for an extra few degrees of insulation.

Use a cold frame to start hardy crops earlier than the open ground allows. Sowings of lettuce, spinach, and early carrots made under the protection of the closed frame come up weeks ahead of the same seed in an exposed, cold bed outside.

Watch the watering in a closed cold frame, because the still, sheltered air can stay damp and breed mould. Water sparingly in cool weather, ventilate whenever the day allows, and the airflow keeps grey mould off the soft growth crowded inside.

A cold frame extends the autumn harvest as the open garden shuts down. Lettuces, herbs, and other tender salads moved into the frame, or sown there in late summer, keep cropping well after the first frosts have flattened everything outside.

Build a simple cold frame from a timber box topped with an old window or a sheet of clear plastic on a hinged frame. It need not be elaborate; even a few straw bales arranged in a rectangle with a pane laid across the top works for a single season.
Slope the lid of a cold frame, with the back higher than the front. The angle sheds rain, sheds snow, and tilts the glass to catch more of the low winter sun, all of which a flat top does poorly.

Move tender pot plants such as pelargoniums into a cold frame to overwinter where a greenhouse is lacking. Kept on the dry side and given the frame's shelter from frost, they survive the cold months and are ready to start back into growth in spring.

Ornamental grasses bring movement to a border that no other plant can. The slightest breeze sets them shimmering and swaying, and a planting of grasses turns a still picture into a living one that catches the eye all season long.

Know whether your grass is a cool-season or a warm-season grower before you cut it back. Cool-season grasses grow early and are best trimmed in late winter, while warm-season grasses come into their own in summer and can be cut hard in early spring.

Comb the dead leaves out of an evergreen grass each spring rather than cutting it down. Run gloved fingers or a rake through the clump to pull away the brown, tired growth, leaving the living foliage to carry on undisturbed.

Leave the seedheads and foliage of deciduous grasses standing through winter. Bleached to straw and rimed with frost, they hold their structure for months, catch the low winter light, and shelter insects, where a tidy autumn cut leaves only bare ground.

Grasses generally want a sunny, open position and a soil that drains freely. Most resent a rich, wet root run, which makes them flop, and the lean conditions that would starve a leafy perennial produce the tightest, most upright grass clumps.

Plant grasses in generous drifts and let them weave between flowering perennials. A grass used as a single dot looks lost, but a river of one kind threading through a border ties the whole planting together and softens the bolder shapes around it.

Lift and divide a clump-forming grass in spring once it grows congested or starts to die out in the centre. Slice the clump apart, discard the worn-out middle, and replant the vigorous outer sections to renew the plant and increase your stock.

Some grasses, particularly the running types, spread aggressively by underground rhizomes and can colonize a border. Confine a known spreader to a sunken container, or stick to the well-behaved clump-formers, and the grass garden stays a pleasure rather than a battle.

Backlight is a grass at its most beautiful. Site grasses where the low morning or evening sun will shine through the flowering heads from behind, and the whole clump lights up in a halo that a plant in flat front-light never achieves.

Many grasses save their best show for late summer and autumn, throwing up their flowering plumes just as the flower border begins to fade. Planting plenty of them carries colour, texture, and interest right through to the first hard frosts.

An espalier trains an apple or pear flat against a wall or wires in a formal pattern of horizontal tiers. It is a productive way to grow fruit in a narrow strip, and the warmth of a sunny wall behind ripens the crop beautifully.

Start an espalier with a young, unbranched maiden tree, called a whip. Cut it just above the height of the first wire so it throws out the shoots that will become the first tier and the new vertical leader, giving you the basic framework to build on.

Choose an apple on a dwarfing or semi-dwarfing rootstock for an espalier. A vigorous rootstock fights the restricting training and floods the tree with growth you must forever cut away, while a dwarfing stock keeps the tree biddable and fruitful within its frame.

Build the espalier one tier a year. In summer tie in the two shoots that form the new horizontal arms and the leader for the next storey, prune the rest, and over four or five seasons the tree rises tier by tier to its finished height.

Summer pruning is the key to a fruitful espalier. Shortening the side shoots in mid to late summer checks excess growth and encourages the formation of fruiting spurs along the trained arms, which a winter prune alone would not achieve.

Train the new arms gradually toward the horizontal rather than tying them flat all at once. Lower a growing shoot a little at a time over the season; pulled down too sharply too soon it may snap, and tied too steeply it grows away too strongly.

Tie the espalier's branches to horizontal wires stretched tight between sturdy posts or fixed off a wall on vine eyes. Space the wires about eighteen inches apart for the tiers, and check the ties each year so they do not cut into the thickening wood.

An espalier needs little ground, so it suits a small garden, and it makes a handsome living screen along a path or boundary. Trained on free-standing wires it divides the garden into rooms while still earning its keep with a crop of fruit.

Pick a spur-bearing apple variety for an espalier, not a tip-bearer. The training relies on a system of short fruiting spurs along the horizontal arms, and a tip-bearer, which fruits at the ends of its shoots, simply will not crop under this regime.

Once an espalier has filled its allotted frame, prune it firmly every summer to hold it there. The tree will always try to grow beyond its bounds, so the annual cutting back of new extension growth is the price of keeping the pattern crisp and the tree productive.

A wormery turns kitchen scraps into rich compost and a liquid feed using composting worms, which are not the earthworms of the garden but surface-dwelling species like the tiger worm. They live and feed in the top layer of decaying matter rather than burrowing in soil.

Feed a wormery little and often, adding a fresh handful of scraps only once the previous lot is being worked over. Overload it and the uneaten food rots, turns acidic, and sours the bin, while a steady measured supply keeps the worms thriving and the bin sweet.

Worms have preferences. They relish soft vegetable and fruit peelings, tea leaves, and coffee grounds, but go easy on citrus and onion, which are too acidic in quantity, and keep out meat, dairy, and anything oily, which putrefies and attracts pests.

Tear or shred cardboard, paper, and egg cartons into the wormery alongside the food scraps. This bedding material soaks up excess moisture, adds the carbon that balances the wet greens, and gives the worms structure and air in which to move and work.

A wormery should smell of clean, earthy soil. A foul, sour stink means it has gone wrong, usually too wet, too acidic, or overfed, and the cure is to stop adding food, mix in plenty of dry shredded paper, and let the worms catch up.

Keep a wormery out of both blazing sun and hard frost, since the worms work best in a moderate, steady temperature. A shed, a garage, or a shaded sheltered spot suits them, and in a cold snap they slow right down and need little feeding.

The dark liquid that drains from the bottom of a wormery is a potent plant food. Dilute it well, until it is the colour of weak tea, before watering it onto plants, because used neat it is far too strong and can scorch the roots.

Harvest the finished worm castings by pushing the worked material to one side of the bin and adding fresh bedding and food to the empty side. The worms migrate across to the new food over a few weeks, leaving the crumbly compost ready to lift out worm-free.

Worm compost is rich, dark, and full of plant nutrients and beneficial microbes. Use it sparingly as a concentrated soil improver, a few handfuls dug into a planting hole or scattered as a top dressing, rather than as a bulk mulch.

A wormery is the ideal composting solution where space is tight. It fits on a balcony or in a small yard, processes a household's vegetable waste quietly and without a heap, and asks for nothing more than a regular feed and the odd handful of paper.

Lay a path wide enough for its purpose. A main route through the garden should take a wheelbarrow comfortably, around three feet at least, while a secondary path between beds need only carry a walker, but a path too narrow to use easily soon becomes no path at all.

A bed edged with a crisp, defined line looks cared for even when the planting is loose. A clean cut between lawn and border, a band of brick, or a length of timber stops grass and plants from blurring into one another and makes mowing and weeding far easier.

Bed gravel paths onto a firm, compacted base of crushed stone, not straight onto soft soil. Without that foundation the gravel sinks into the ground, the path turns to a muddy scatter, and weeds find the disturbed earth beneath it within a season.

A path of bark chippings or wood chips suits an informal garden, a woodland walk, or the route between vegetable beds. It is soft underfoot, cheap, and weed-suppressing, though it rots down over a few years and needs topping up to stay thick and clean.

An edging board sunk along the side of a gravel or chip path keeps the loose material where it belongs. Without a physical edge the surface slowly creeps out into the borders and lawn, and the path grows thin and ragged at its margins.

Set stepping stones across a lawn or border at an easy stride apart, slightly sunk so the mower can pass straight over them. Spaced at a natural walking pace they save the grass from being worn into a muddy track and lead the eye through the garden.

A path of laid bricks or stone setts on a proper base is permanent and handsome, repaying its higher cost and effort with decades of clean, firm, all-weather use. Lay the units with a slight fall to one side so rain drains off rather than pooling.

Plant low, spreading herbs like creeping thyme or chamomile into the joints of a path or among stepping stones. Crushed underfoot they release their scent, and a fragrant path turns an everyday walk to the shed into a small daily pleasure.

Give a path a slight camber or a gentle cross-fall so water sheds off it. A perfectly flat path holds puddles, grows slippery with algae, and stays sodden after rain, while one that drains stays usable and safe in all weathers.

A curving path leads the eye onward and makes a garden feel larger and more inviting than a straight line that reveals everything at once. Sweep the path behind a planting so its destination is hidden, and the garden gains a sense of mystery and journey.

Plant single, open-faced flowers for the bees rather than blowsy doubles. A simple daisy, poppy, or single dahlia offers an easy landing pad and an open dish of accessible nectar and pollen, while a tightly petalled double often hides or lacks its reward.

Aim for an unbroken chain of bloom from early spring to late autumn. Crocus and pulmonaria feed the first bees on the wing, summer is easy, and late asters, sedums, and ivy carry the pollinators through to the colder days when little else is open.

Bees see ultraviolet, blue, and purple most clearly, so a drift of lavender, catmint, salvia, or borage acts as a beacon. Planting plenty of these blue and purple flowers draws far more pollinators than the same area scattered with mixed colours.

Plant in bold blocks of a single kind rather than dotting flowers about singly. A bee working a patch of one plant can forage efficiently without flying far between flowers, and a generous drift is far more attractive to passing pollinators than a thin scatter.

Different pollinators need different flower shapes. Long-tongued bumblebees and moths reach deep into tubular foxgloves and honeysuckle, while short-tongued bees and hoverflies need the shallow, open flowers of the daisy and umbellifer families. Plant a mix to feed them all.

Let some herbs and vegetables run to flower for the pollinators. The flowers of thyme, oregano, chives, and a bolting brassica are all magnets for bees, so leaving a few plants to bloom rather than pulling them turns the kitchen garden into forage.

Night-flowering and pale, scented flowers feed the moths, the unsung pollinators of the dark hours. Evening primrose, honeysuckle, and night-scented stock open and release their perfume as the sun goes down, drawing in moths long after the bees have gone to roost.

A few weeds and wildflowers among the cultivated planting are a feast for pollinators. Dandelions are one of the earliest reliable sources of nectar in the year, and a strip of clover, knapweed, or bird's-foot trefoil left to bloom feeds insects the borders cannot.

Pollinators need water as well as nectar. A shallow dish filled with pebbles or marbles and topped up with water gives bees a safe place to land and drink without drowning, a small addition that helps them through a hot, dry spell.

Skip the pesticides where you are gardening for pollinators, because an insecticide makes no distinction between a pest and a bee. Even systemic chemicals can taint the nectar and pollen of a treated plant, so a flower meant to feed bees should never be sprayed.

Hardening off is the gradual toughening of an indoor-raised seedling so it can survive outdoors. A plant moved straight from a warm windowsill into the open garden suffers a brutal check from wind, sun, and cold that a slow transition prevents.

Begin hardening off about a week or two before planting out. Set the seedlings outside in a sheltered, lightly shaded spot for an hour or two on the first day, and lengthen their time outdoors a little each day as they adjust.

Bring tender seedlings back under cover each night during the early days of hardening off, or move them into a cold frame whose lid you can close. They are not ready for a cold night outside, and a sudden chill can undo days of careful acclimatizing.

A cold frame makes hardening off simple. Stand the seedlings in the closed frame, then over the following days prop the lid open a little wider each day and for longer, until at last it stays off altogether and the plants are ready for the open ground.

Watch the weather while hardening off and keep the plants in on a day of cold wind, heavy rain, or harsh sun. The whole point is a gentle transition, and exposing soft seedlings to a violent day sets them back further than skipping it would.

Ease back a little on the watering as you harden off seedlings, letting them grow slightly more accustomed to the drier, less coddled life of the garden. A plant kept lush and pampered to the last minute struggles more with the move than one toughened gradually.

Skipping the hardening off stage is a common and costly mistake. A pampered seedling planted straight out often turns pale, scorched, and stunted within days, sometimes never recovering, while a hardened plant of the same age takes the move in its stride.

Hardened-off seedlings look subtly different from soft indoor ones. Their leaves are a little smaller, thicker, and a deeper green, their stems sturdier, and that tougher, less luxuriant appearance is exactly the sign that they are ready for the garden.

Plant out hardened seedlings on a dull, still, or showery day rather than in bright sun and drying wind. The gentle conditions let the plant settle its roots into the new soil without the added stress of heat and water loss in its first hours outdoors.

Even hardened-off plants appreciate a little help in their first week outside. A cloche, a temporary windbreak, or a light drape of fleece eases the final transition, and is cheap insurance against an unexpected cold snap catching the young plants out.

An arch or pergola lifts climbing plants overhead and turns flat garden space into a third dimension. A rose or a vine trained over an arch frames a view, marks the passage from one part of the garden to another, and clothes the air above the path with flower.

An obelisk gives a climber a free-standing pillar of support in the middle of a border. It draws the eye upward, adds height where a flat planting would be dull, and a sweet pea or clematis spiralling up it makes a vertical exclamation mark among the lower plants.

A trellis fixed to a wall must stand a little clear of the brickwork on battens. The gap lets air circulate behind the plant, gives a twining climber something to wrap around, and keeps the foliage from being pressed flat and airless against the wall.

Grow vegetables upward to multiply a small plot. Climbing beans, cucumbers, and even small squash trained up netting, a tripod, or a trellis crop heavily in a tiny footprint, and lifting them off the ground keeps the produce clean and the picking easy on the back.

Match the strength of the support to the eventual weight of the plant. A mature wisteria or a vigorous rambling rose is astonishingly heavy and will pull down a flimsy structure, so build for the plant it will become, not the slip you are planting now.

A tripod or wigwam of canes is the quickest vertical support there is. Three or more stout canes pushed into the soil and tied at the top make an instant climbing frame for beans or sweet peas, and it can be put up and taken down with the season.

Distinguish a self-clinging climber from one that needs tying in. Ivy and climbing hydrangea grip a wall by themselves with aerial roots, while a clematis, a rose, or a honeysuckle has no such hold and must be guided onto and fastened to its support.

A green wall or living wall of planted pockets clothes a bare vertical surface in foliage and flower. It demands reliable irrigation, since the small soil pockets dry fast, but it brings growth and life to a spot where no plant could otherwise root.

Train a climber out to cover its whole support, not just race to the top. Spread and tie in the young shoots horizontally and at an angle; left to their own devices most climbers bolt straight up and flower only at the summit, leaving a bare and leggy base.

A pergola clothed in a leafy climber casts a dappled shade that turns a patio into a cool outdoor room. A deciduous vine is ideal, giving shade through the summer heat and then dropping its leaves to let the welcome low sun through in winter.

Resist the urge to strip the garden bare in autumn. Leaving seedheads, hollow stems, and a layer of fallen leaves provides food and shelter for birds and overwintering insects, and a garden tidied to the bone is a garden empty of the life that controls its pests.

Gather fallen leaves into a wire cage or a stack of old bags and let them rot down into leaf mould. It takes a year or two, but the dark, crumbly result is a superb soil conditioner and mulch, and it costs nothing but the raking.

Lift tender plants such as dahlias, cannas, and pelargoniums before the first hard frost can kill them. Store the dahlia tubers and canna rhizomes somewhere cool and frost-free, and bring the pelargoniums under cover, and they will see you through to spring.

Clear away any plant material that was diseased through the season and do not compost it. Blighted potato haulm, rose leaves spotted with black spot, and mildewed stems should be burned or binned, since a cool heap will not kill the spores and you would only spread them.

Rake fallen leaves off the lawn so they do not lie in a sodden mat that smothers and yellows the grass beneath. The leaves are no waste, though; raked onto the borders or stacked to make leaf mould, they are a resource rather than a chore.

Autumn is the time to lift and divide overcrowded herbaceous perennials. The soil is still warm enough for roots to establish, the plants are slowing toward dormancy, and a clump split now is settled and ready to romp away the moment spring arrives.

Empty, clean, and store away the season's containers, canes, and supports. Scrubbing the pots removes pests and disease that would overwinter in the crust of old compost, and bringing terracotta and ceramic under cover saves it from cracking in a hard frost.

Plant spring-flowering bulbs as part of the autumn round of work. Tucking daffodils, crocus, and tulips into the ground now, while clearing the spent summer planting, means a welcome show of colour after the long winter with no further effort.

Mulch the bare soil of cleared beds before winter rather than leaving it open. A layer of compost or well-rotted manure protects the soil structure from being beaten down by winter rain, feeds the soil life, and is drawn down ready for spring planting.

Give the tools a proper end-of-season clean before they go into store. Scrape and oil the metal, treat the wooden handles, sharpen the edges, and service the mower, so that everything is ready to work the moment the first fine days of spring arrive.

Most supermarket orchids are moth orchids, and the commonest way they die is from a sodden, rotted root. Water only when the potting bark is nearly dry, and tip away any water that collects in the saucer rather than leaving the pot standing in it.

A moth orchid wants bright but filtered light, never harsh direct sun. An east-facing windowsill is close to ideal, and a leaf that flushes yellowish or feels hot to the touch is telling you the light is too strong and the plant needs a gentler spot.

Pot an orchid in coarse bark, not ordinary compost. The thick, fleshy aerial roots need air around them as much as moisture, and the open, chunky bark gives them both, while dense potting soil suffocates the roots and they slowly rot.

After a moth orchid finishes flowering, do not cut the green stem right down. Trim it back to a node below the lowest faded flower and the plant will often branch and bloom again from that point within a few months, given warmth and good light.

Feed an orchid weakly but regularly through its growing season with a dilute orchid fertilizer. The bark holds few nutrients of its own, so a quarter-strength feed every second or third watering keeps the plant in good heart without scorching the roots.

Healthy orchid roots are plump and silvery-green, turning a brighter green when wet. Roots that are brown, soft, and mushy have rotted from overwatering, while shrivelled, papery roots mean the plant has been left too dry for too long.

Repot an orchid every couple of years once the bark has broken down into a fine, water-holding sludge. Decayed bark holds too much moisture and starves the roots of air, and fresh chunky bark in a clear pot restores the open conditions the plant needs.

A clear plastic pot suits a moth orchid well. It lets you see the state of the roots at a glance, and since the roots themselves photosynthesize a little, the light reaching them through the transparent pot does the plant no harm at all.

Many orchids are nudged into flowering by a drop in night temperature. A spell of cooler nights in autumn, a difference of several degrees from the daytime warmth, often triggers a reluctant moth orchid to set the spike it has been withholding.

Stake an orchid's flower spike as it lengthens, tying it loosely to a thin cane. Supporting the spike before the buds open keeps the arching stem from snapping under the weight of the flowers and holds the blooms in a graceful, well-displayed arc.

Blueberries demand an acidic soil, somewhere around pH four and a half to five and a half, and will slowly starve and yellow in a neutral or limey ground. If your garden soil is not naturally acidic, the surest route to a crop is to grow them in pots of ericaceous compost.

Water blueberries with rainwater wherever you can, especially in a hard-water area. Tap water carries dissolved lime that, applied over months, gradually pushes the soil pH up out of the acidic range the plants need and undoes your careful soil preparation.

Plant two or more different blueberry varieties for the heaviest crop. Although many are partly self-fertile, cross-pollination between varieties markedly improves the fruit set and produces larger berries than a single lonely bush ever will.

Blueberries fruit on wood that is two or three years old. Once a bush is mature, prune out the oldest, twiggiest, least productive stems each winter to make room for vigorous young growth, keeping the bush in a constant cycle of renewal.

Net blueberry bushes as the fruit colours, because birds will strip a crop with astonishing speed. Drape the netting over a frame so it does not touch the berries, and tuck it in firmly at the base so a hungry blackbird cannot creep underneath.

Mulch blueberries generously with an acidic material such as pine bark, pine needles, or composted leaves. The mulch keeps their shallow, fibrous roots cool and moist, suppresses weeds that would compete, and slowly maintains the acidity they crave.

Blueberries have shallow root systems that resent both drought and waterlogging. They need a steady, even supply of moisture, particularly through the weeks when the fruit is swelling, so never let a fruiting bush dry out at that critical stage.

Do not let a young blueberry bush fruit too heavily in its first year or two. Removing some or all of the early flowers steers the plant's energy into building a strong framework of branches and roots, which pays off in far larger crops later.

Pick blueberries a few days after they turn fully blue rather than the moment they colour. The berry keeps sweetening for a while after it goes blue, and a berry that drops into the hand at the lightest touch is at its ripest and best.

Blueberry foliage blazes a brilliant red and orange in autumn, and the bare red-twigged stems have their own quiet beauty in winter. The bush earns its place as an ornamental shrub, so it need not be hidden away in the fruit cage.

Late winter is for planning and the earliest sowings under cover. Order seed, prepare the beds the moment they are workable, and start slow crops like onions and the first tomatoes indoors with warmth, ready for the longer days that are coming.

Early spring sees the soil begin to warm and the sowing season open in earnest. Hardy vegetables can go directly into the ground, more tender crops are started under glass, and the whole garden shifts from planning into action.

By late spring the risk of frost has passed in most gardens, and the tender plants raised indoors can at last be hardened off and planted out. It is the busiest moment of the gardening year, with both sowing and planting in full swing.

Early summer is a time of succession sowing and steady maintenance. Keep sowing salad crops and beans in short, frequent batches for a continuous supply, stake and tie the growing plants, and stay ahead of the weeds while they are still small.

High summer is for harvesting, watering, and feeding rather than fresh sowing, though a few autumn and winter crops are started now. Keep the cropping plants picked and watered, and the garden rewards the effort with its heaviest yields.

Late summer turns the gardener's mind toward the seasons ahead. Sow hardy salads and overwintering vegetables, order spring bulbs, take cuttings of tender plants, and begin to think about the slow shutting-down of the productive year.

Autumn is the great planting season for anything woody. The soil is still warm, the air is cool and damp, and a tree, shrub, or perennial set out now establishes its roots over the dormant months and races away in spring.

Plant spring-flowering bulbs through autumn, daffodils early and tulips later once the ground has cooled. Tucking them in now, while clearing the fading summer beds, banks a display of colour to be drawn on after the long winter.

Winter is the season for the structural jobs. Prune dormant apples and pears, take hardwood cuttings, dig over heavy ground for the frost to break down, mend the fences, service the tools, and pore over the seed catalogues for the year to come.

Sow and plant in tune with your own garden, not a fixed national date. A sheltered southern plot runs weeks ahead of a cold northern one, and the only reliable guide is your soil's temperature and the average date of your last and first frosts.

Plant a bare-root hedge in the dormant season, from late autumn through winter into early spring. Bare-root whips are cheap, establish quickly, and a hedge planted this way, while the plants are leafless and asleep, settles in far better than a costly potted alternative.

Space hedge plants according to how dense and how fast a screen you want. Setting the whips close together, even in a staggered double row, gives a thick hedge sooner, while wider spacing is cheaper but takes longer to knit into a solid wall of growth.

Cut a new hedge back hard after planting, even though it feels wrong to do so. Reducing the height of the young whips forces them to branch low and bushy from the base, and that early hard prune is what prevents a thin, gappy, leggy hedge in later years.

Trim a formal hedge with the sides sloping gently inward toward the top, a shape called a batter. The narrower top lets light reach the lower branches, which would otherwise be shaded out and go bare, and it also helps the hedge shrug off heavy snow.

Check a hedge for nesting birds before you trim it through the breeding season. Disturbing or destroying an active nest is both unkind and, in many places, against the law, so leave the shears in the shed from spring until the young have safely fledged.

A formal evergreen hedge usually needs cutting two or three times through the growing season to stay crisp. A vigorous deciduous hedge may want a couple of trims a year, while an informal flowering hedge is cut just once, after it has bloomed.

Feed and mulch a hedge, especially a young one, just as you would any other planting. A hedge is a row of hardworking shrubs growing close together and competing fiercely for water and nutrients, and it cannot thrive on neglect alone.

Renovate an overgrown, bare-bottomed deciduous hedge by cutting it back hard in winter, taking one side one year and the other the next. Hawthorn, beech, and hornbeam respond to this drastic treatment by breaking afresh from the old wood and thickening up again.

A native mixed hedge of hawthorn, blackthorn, hazel, and field maple does far more than a single-species formal one. It feeds and shelters birds and insects, gives blossom and berry through the year, and asks only a single light trim each season.

Use sharp, clean shears or a well-maintained powered trimmer, and run a taut string line as a guide for the top of a formal hedge. A straight, level cut against a line gives the crisp result that makes a clipped hedge look deliberate rather than merely hacked.

Chit early potatoes before planting by standing the seed tubers in a cool, bright, frost-free place for a few weeks. They sprout short, sturdy, dark-green shoots, and a chitted tuber gets away faster once in the ground, bringing the harvest forward.

Plant seed potatoes once the worst of the frost is past, setting them in a trench or individual holes with the sprouts pointing upward. Early varieties go in first, maincrop later, spaced further apart since they grow into much larger plants.

Earth up potato plants as the shoots grow, drawing soil up around the stems to bury the lower leaves. This keeps developing tubers covered and stops them greening in the light, and the growing ridge also gives a measure of protection from late frost.

Green potatoes are poisonous and must not be eaten. Tubers exposed to light, whether in the ground, in storage, or on the kitchen shelf, turn green and develop bitter toxins, so keep them earthed up while growing and stored in the dark afterwards.

Lift first early potatoes as soon as the plants come into flower, when the tubers are small, waxy, and at their most delicious. There is no need to harvest the whole row at once; dig each plant as you want it and the rest keep growing in the ground.

Maincrop potatoes for storing are left in the ground until the foliage, the haulm, has died back in late summer or autumn. Cut the haulm down, leave the tubers a fortnight to set their skins firm, then lift them on a dry day for the store.

Potato blight, the disease that caused historic famines, strikes in warm, humid summer weather, browning the foliage and rotting the tubers. Choose blight-resistant varieties, grow earlies that crop before blight usually arrives, and cut and remove infected haulm at once.

Potatoes crop perfectly well in a large container, a sack, or a sturdy bag for the gardener short of ground. Plant a few tubers in a deep pot, keep adding compost as the shoots grow, water generously, and tip the whole lot out to harvest.

Always plant certified seed potatoes rather than tubers saved from the kitchen or last year's crop. Certified seed is grown to be free of the viruses and diseases that build up in saved stock and would otherwise be carried into your soil.

Store lifted maincrop potatoes in the dark in paper or hessian sacks, never sealed plastic, somewhere cool but frost-free. They need to breathe, and kept dark, dry, and cold they will hold sound and edible right through the winter months.

Choose compact and dwarf vegetable varieties bred for containers and small spaces. Bush tomatoes, patio aubergines, dwarf beans, and baby-leaf salads crop generously in a pot, where their full-sized cousins would sprawl beyond what a patio can hold.

Pick the largest pot you can accommodate, because a bigger volume of compost holds water and nutrients longer and rides out a hot day far better than a small one. A cramped pot dries out twice as fast and keeps the plant forever on the edge of stress.

Salad leaves are the perfect crop for a patio container. Sown thickly in a shallow trough and cut young as a cut-and-come-again crop, they give weeks of fresh leaves from a small space and regrow two or three times before the row is exhausted.

Group containers together on a patio and they shelter and shade one another, slowing the rate at which they dry out. A clustered arrangement is also easier to water, easier to feed, and far more pleasing to the eye than pots scattered about singly.

Feed container vegetables regularly through the season, because the small reservoir of compost is soon exhausted and every watering flushes nutrients away. A weekly liquid feed, switching to a high-potash one once fruit sets, keeps a patio crop productive.

Stand a few herbs in pots right by the kitchen door for the easiest harvest in the garden. Parsley, chives, mint, and basil within arm's reach get used constantly, and a clutch of herb pots is the most rewarding container planting a cook can grow.

Strawberries thrive in patio pots, tubs, and hanging baskets, and growing them off the ground keeps the fruit clean and out of reach of slugs. The good drainage of a container suits them well, provided the watering is steady while the berries swell.

A growbag is a ready-made container for hungry crops like tomatoes, peppers, and cucumbers on a patio. Cut planting holes in the top, pierce the base for drainage, and a single bag will carry two or three plants through a productive summer.

Vegetables in containers need more frequent watering than anything in open ground, sometimes twice a day in high summer. A self-watering pot with a built-in reservoir, or a simple drip line on a timer, takes the daily anxiety out of a patio crop.

Make use of the vertical space on a balcony or patio. A trellis against the wall, a tiered stand, or a wall-mounted planter lets you grow climbing beans, trailing tomatoes, and tumbling strawberries upward, multiplying the harvest from a tiny floor area.

The single most useful thing a gardener can do for almost any soil is to add organic matter. Garden compost, well-rotted manure, and leaf mould improve a heavy clay and a light sand alike, and a yearly dressing builds fertility and life over time.

Organic matter helps opposite soils in opposite ways. Worked into a sticky clay it opens the structure and improves drainage; spread on a thirsty sand it acts like a sponge and helps the soil hold both water and nutrients. The same compost cures both faults.

Identify your soil before you try to improve it. Rub a moist sample between finger and thumb: a clay soil feels sticky and smears smooth, a sandy one feels gritty and falls apart, and a loam, the gardener's ideal, sits comfortably between the two.

Avoid digging or even walking on soil when it is wet, particularly a clay. Working a sodden soil destroys the crumb structure, smearing and compacting it into an airless mass, and a clay damaged this way sets like concrete and is the devil to recover.

The no-dig approach builds soil from the top down. Rather than turning the ground over, a layer of compost is spread on the surface each year and the worms and soil life draw it down, preserving the soil's structure and the network of fungi within it.

A green manure sown on bare ground protects and feeds the soil. The crop covers the surface against erosion, holds nutrients that rain would wash away, and is dug in or cut down before it seeds, returning all that growth to the soil as it rots.

Worms are the best indicator of a healthy soil. A spadeful of good ground turns up plenty of them, and their constant burrowing aerates the soil, drains it, and mixes organic matter through it. A soil rich in worms needs little other help.

Test the soil before adding lime or fertilizer, because guesswork wastes money and can do harm. A simple test reveals the pH and the nutrients actually present, letting you correct what is genuinely lacking rather than dosing the ground blindly.

Grit, coarse sand, or fine gravel forked into a heavy clay improves its drainage, but only if added in real quantity alongside organic matter. A token sprinkle does nothing; it takes a generous, well-mixed dose to make a lasting difference to the structure.

Improving a soil is the work of years, not a single weekend. Each annual mulch of compost, each green manure, each spadeful that is not dug when wet, adds a little, and a soil tended patiently grows steadily darker, richer, and easier to work.

Light a garden gently and sparingly after dark. A few well-placed pools of soft light pick out a tree, a path, or a seating area far more beautifully than a single harsh floodlight that flattens the whole garden and drowns out the stars.

Use uplighting to dramatize a specimen tree or a striking plant. A spotlight set low at the base and angled upward throws the branching structure into relief against the night sky, turning a daytime feature into a piece of evening sculpture.

Light the steps, the path edges, and any change of level for safety as much as beauty. Low, downward-facing markers along a route let people move through the garden after dark without stumbling, and a path lit this way invites an evening stroll.

Solar lights are simple to install with no wiring at all, charging by day and glowing softly by night, though their light is gentle and they fade in a run of dull weather. For a brighter, more reliable display, a low-voltage wired system is the better choice.

Choose a warm white light over a cold blue-white one for a garden. Warm light flatters foliage and flowers, casts a welcoming glow, and feels restful, where a harsh cold light makes plants look grey and lifeless and the space clinical.

Mind the wildlife when lighting a garden. Bright lights left on all night disturb the moths, bats, and other creatures that depend on the dark, so use lights only where and when they are needed, on a timer or a sensor rather than burning till dawn.

A string of soft fairy lights through a tree or along a pergola, or a cluster of candles and lanterns on a table, gives an outdoor seating area instant atmosphere. Such gentle, decorative light makes a patio feel like a room for a summer evening.

Conceal the light source and let people see only its effect. A fitting tucked behind a plant, beneath a step, or among the foliage casts its glow without glaring into the eye, and the garden seems lit by magic rather than by visible fixtures.

Light water and it doubles its charm after dark. A discreet light playing on a pond, a fountain, or a small cascade catches the movement and the reflections, and the sound and sparkle of lit water become the heart of the evening garden.

Less is almost always more with garden lighting. Start with a single light on the most important feature, live with it for a while, and add another only where the garden genuinely calls for it. An over-lit garden loses all its evening mystery.

Learn to tell an annual weed from a perennial one, because they need different treatment. An annual like chickweed is easily hoed off before it seeds, while a perennial like bindweed or couch grass regrows from every scrap of root left behind.

Hoe annual weeds off on a warm, dry day while they are still tiny seedlings. Slicing them through at the soil surface in dry weather leaves them to wither and die in the sun, and a few minutes' hoeing now saves hours of hand-weeding later.

Never let a weed set seed. The old saying that one year's seeding makes seven years' weeding holds true, since a single plant can shed thousands of seeds that lie dormant in the soil for years, so pull or hoe a weed before it ever flowers.

Dig out perennial weeds like dandelion and dock with as much of the long taproot as you can. Any fragment of root left in the ground will sprout afresh, so patient, thorough removal beats a quick snap of the leaves that leaves the root to regrow.

Smother a badly infested patch by covering it for a season with thick cardboard, old carpet, or black plastic. Deprived of all light, even tough perennial weeds eventually weaken and die, and the cleared ground can then be planted without a chemical in sight.

A thick mulch is the gardener's most peaceful weapon against weeds. Spread two or three inches deep over clean soil it blocks the light that weed seeds need to germinate, and a well-mulched bed stays clean with only the lightest occasional hand-weeding.

Tackle perennial weeds when their roots are at their weakest. Repeatedly cutting down the top growth of a plant like bindweed forces it to keep drawing on its root reserves to regrow, and persistent removal will eventually exhaust and starve it out.

The fastest way to keep a bed weed-free is to fill it with plants. Bare soil is an open invitation that weeds will accept, while a densely planted border or a carpet of ground cover leaves them no light, no room, and no foothold to colonize.

Some so-called weeds are worth tolerating in the right place. A clump of nettles feeds butterfly caterpillars, dandelions are early forage for bees, and a patch of clover fixes nitrogen, so a corner left a little wild can be an asset rather than a failing.

Weed after rain, when the soil is soft and moist and the roots draw out whole and unbroken. A weed pulled from dry, hard ground usually snaps off at the neck, leaving the root behind to grow again, while damp soil yields up the whole plant.
